subtype: Approach: working backward from the exam date [Thinking]
passage: Swati, you asked why I dropped two optional topics from my plan. I'll show you the maths. I'm Anjali. On 1 January I counted: the exam is on 24 May. That's twenty weeks. I wanted the last four weeks only for revision, and before that three weeks of full mocks. So twenty minus seven: thirteen weeks for learning the syllabus. Ninety-one days. Then I listed the blocks: polity, history, geography, economy, environment, science, current affairs, and my optional. When I divided, each block got about eleven days. History alone needs twenty, honestly. I sat there feeling a bit sick. The plan didn't fit. So I had to cut. I combined environment with geography, trimmed science to the basics, and dropped two rarely asked optional topics. It hurt. But a plan that doesn't fit isn't a plan. It's a wish.

qa.q: When is the exam?
qa.a: The exam is on 24 May.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel on seeing eleven days per block?
qa.a: Anjali felt a bit sick and worried, realising the plan didn't fit and something had to be cut.

qa.q: What else could Anjali do to make the cuts safer?
qa.a: Anjali could check past papers to see which topics are rarely asked, so the cuts fall on low-value areas.

qa.q: How might Swati see Anjali's cuts?
qa.a: Swati, who asked why topics were dropped, gets a clear reason rooted in the dates, which may help Swati check a plan of Swati's own.

grounding: Shows a candidate counting weeks to the exam, subtracting revision and mock periods, and seeing how few days each syllabus block gets, so the plan needs a cut.

subtype: Approach: working backward from the exam date [Thinking]
passage: I'm Devika, Mehak's flatmate, and last Sunday I watched her plan the whole exam year on our kitchen wall. She stuck up a sheet of chart paper and wrote the exam date at the far right: 15 June. Then she counted back the weeks under her breath and wrote "22". She marked the last three weeks in red: "Only revising." The three before that in blue: "Mocks." That left sixteen weeks. She listed her subjects down the side, nine of them, and started dividing. I heard her mutter, "Twelve days for modern history? That's a joke." She stood back for a long time. Then she picked up a pen and crossed out a whole column labelled "Extra reading" and one optional topic. I can't say what she felt; she just said, "Okay. Now it fits," and went to make tea.

qa.q: What date did Mehak write for the exam?
qa.a: 15 June.

qa.q: What might Mehak have felt when she muttered about twelve days?
qa.a: Mehak was probably frustrated and worried, seeing that the time left for each subject was too little.

qa.q: What else could Mehak do after cutting?
qa.a: Mehak could check every four weeks whether each block is on time, and adjust before the revision weeks are threatened.

qa.q: How does Devika see the planning?
qa.a: Devika watches closely but only guesses at Mehak's feelings, noticing the long pause before the cuts and the calm now it fits.

grounding: Illustrates a candidate counting back from the exam date, setting aside revision and mock weeks, and cutting the plan once the days per subject look too few.

subtype: Approach: prioritising by marks weightage [Thinking]
passage: In the coaching institute's library, Disha had spread out ten years of past papers for the state engineering services exam. Lalit, from her batch, pulled up a chair. "Past papers already? We haven't finished the syllabus." "I'm not solving them," she said. "I'm counting." She had made a table: every question, its topic, its marks. Some topics came up every single year: strength of materials, fluid mechanics, surveying. Together they were almost forty percent of the marks. Others, like one small chapter on tunnel ventilation, had appeared twice in ten years. Lalit looked at her study order. "So you're starting with the big three." "And leaving the rare ones for the last month. If I run out of time, I lose two marks, not forty." Lalit took a photo of her table. "Can I copy the method?"

qa.q: How many years of past papers did Disha spread out?
qa.a: Ten years of past papers.

qa.q: How does Disha feel about her order of study?
qa.a: Disha feels confident and calm about it, knowing that running short of time would cost only a few marks.

qa.q: What else could Disha add to the plan?
qa.a: Disha could rate her own strength in each big topic, so the heaviest and weakest areas get the most time.

qa.q: How does Lalit react to Disha's table?
qa.a: Lalit is surprised at first but quickly sees the sense, taking a photo and asking to copy the method.

grounding: Shows an aspirant analysing past papers to find which topics carry the most marks, starting with those and leaving rarely asked topics for the end.

subtype: Approach: prioritising by marks weightage [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: my new study order (weightage!)
Hi Pallavi,
Remember how I was studying the bank exam syllabus in textbook order? I stopped this week.
I went through the last six years of papers and counted marks by topic. Reasoning was 35 of the 100 prelims marks every year. Quant was 35 too, but mostly data interpretation and arithmetic; probability and permutations together were only about 3 marks a year. English was 30, and reading comprehension was the biggest part.
So my new order: data interpretation and arithmetic first, then puzzles and seating arrangements, then reading comprehension. Probability and the rare stuff go to the last two weeks.
I feel strangely lighter. Before this, I was spending a whole week on permutations, which might give me 2 marks.
Want me to share the tally sheet?
Mahima

qa.q: How many prelims marks was reasoning?
qa.a: Reasoning was 35 of the 100 prelims marks every year.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel after changing the order?
qa.a: Mahima feels strangely lighter, relieved not to spend a whole week on a topic worth so few marks.

qa.q: What else could Mahima check alongside weightage?
qa.a: Mahima could note which high-weight topics are personally weakest and put extra time there first.

qa.q: How might Pallavi use the tally sheet?
qa.a: Pallavi could see at once where the marks are and rethink a study order that follows the textbook.

grounding: Illustrates an aspirant counting marks by topic across past papers and reordering study to start with the heaviest topics and leave rare ones for last.

subtype: Approach: time-boxed daily schedule with fixed slots [Action]
passage: Zubin's timetable for the civil services prelims was taped above his desk in their small Nagpur flat: 7 to 9:30 study, 30-minute break, 10 to 12:30, lunch, 2 to 4:30, walk, 6 to 8, dinner, lights out at 10:30. Sunday evening: one hour to review the week. Then his cousin Ganga's wedding arrived, and the flat filled with relatives, a dholak in the living room, and his mother needing help with everything. Zubin's motivation, already low in the fourth month, sank further. He didn't abandon the timetable. He moved it. The 7 am block went up to the terrace, before anyone woke. The afternoon block shrank to ninety minutes in the building's quiet stairwell. He still slept at 10:30, even on the night of the sangeet, leaving early with a plate of food. On Sunday, reviewing his log, he had kept seventy percent of his hours. Not perfect. Enough.

qa.q: What time is lights out on Zubin's timetable?
qa.a: Lights out at 10:30.

qa.q: How was Zubin feeling during the wedding week?
qa.a: Zubin felt low and unmotivated, already in the fourth month and with the flat full of noise and relatives.

qa.q: What else could Zubin do next time a family event comes?
qa.a: Zubin could plan a lighter version of the timetable for that week in advance, so the change is a choice, not a scramble.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Zubin leaving the sangeet early?
qa.a: Ganga might feel a little sad he left early, but may understand, since he joined in, ate with the family and kept his exam goals.

grounding: Shows an aspirant keeping a daily timetable of study blocks, breaks, fixed sleep and a weekly review, and following it even when motivation dips.

subtype: Approach: time-boxed daily schedule with fixed slots [Action]
passage: In her paying-guest room in Delhi's Mukherjee Nagar, Aparna's day was a grid on the wall: four study blocks of two and a half hours, a thirty-minute break after each, lights out at 11, and a one-hour review every Saturday at 5. Her roommate Aadhya, preparing for the same exam, studied in bursts, sometimes ten hours, sometimes none. In the second month, a grey week came. Aparna woke up heavy, scrolled her phone in bed, and felt no reason to open the polity book. She looked at the grid. "You don't have to feel like it," she told herself. "You just have to sit down at 7." She did. The first hour was slow; by the second she was taking notes. That Saturday, her review showed twenty-six blocks out of twenty-eight done. Aadhya, flat on her bed after another zero day, asked quietly, "Can you make me a grid too?"

qa.q: When is Aparna's weekly review?
qa.a: Every Saturday at 5, for one hour.

qa.q: How was Aparna feeling during the grey week?
qa.a: Aparna felt heavy and unmotivated, scrolling in bed with no wish to open the polity book.

qa.q: What else could help Aparna on low days?
qa.a: Aparna could make the first block of a low day an easier task, like revision, so starting feels lighter while the routine stays.

qa.q: How is Aadhya affected by Aparna's routine?
qa.a: Aadhya, worn out by burst-and-crash days, sees the steady routine working and asks for a grid too.

grounding: Illustrates an aspirant with fixed study blocks, breaks, sleep time and a weekly review who keeps to the grid through a low-motivation week.

subtype: Approach: collecting resources instead of studying [Pitfall]
passage: In their small house in Hisar, Nikita's phone buzzed all day. She had joined fourteen study groups for the bank exams. Every morning she forwarded the best PDFs to her own "Important" folder. By March it held 312 files. She had switched online teachers three times: one was too slow, one too fast, one had a better accent. Her younger brother Anirban watched her scroll. "Didi, which book are you on?" "I'm collecting the best material first. Then I'll study properly." Her mock test that Sunday came back at 38 out of 100. She scrolled back through her notes. Four books started, none finished. The folder of 312 PDFs sat there, most of them unopened. Anirban peeked at the score and quietly put a cup of tea beside her. She didn't forward anything for the rest of the day.

qa.q: How many files were in the Important folder by March?
qa.a: By March it held 312 files.

qa.q: How might Nikita have felt on seeing 38 out of 100?
qa.a: Nikita likely felt shaken and disheartened, seeing that all the collecting hadn't turned into learning.

qa.q: What would you change first in Nikita's approach?
qa.a: Pick one book and one teacher, finish them, and leave most of the groups, so the time goes into studying rather than collecting.

qa.q: How does Anirban respond to the score?
qa.a: Anirban notices her disappointment and quietly brings tea, showing care without adding pressure.

grounding: Shows a candidate joining many groups, downloading dozens of PDFs and switching teachers, feeling busy but never finishing one book, so little is retained.

subtype: Approach: collecting resources instead of studying [Pitfall]
passage: Paulo was preparing for the national civil service exam in Curitiba, and he was always busy. He followed nine study channels, had signed up for three online courses, and saved every summary shared in his exam forums. His laptop desktop was a wall of folders: "Law PDFs", "Law PDFs 2", "Best notes FINAL". Elif, his flatmate, a master's student from Istanbul, watched him download another bundle one evening. "Have you finished any of these?" she asked. Paulo laughed. "Not yet. I'm building my library first." Two months later, a friend quizzed him on administrative law over dinner. He knew the names of five well-known teachers and the titles of eleven books. He couldn't answer three basic questions. That night he opened "Best notes FINAL" and realised he had never read past page six.

qa.q: How many study channels did Paulo follow?
qa.a: He followed nine study channels.

qa.q: How did Paulo feel when he couldn't answer the basic questions?
qa.a: Paulo likely felt embarrassed and shaken, realising he knew about books but not what was in them.

qa.q: What else could Paulo do starting tomorrow?
qa.a: Paulo could choose one course and one book, set the rest aside, and test himself each week without notes.

qa.q: How might Elif see Paulo's library?
qa.a: Elif sees a lot of collecting and very little finishing, which is why her simple question lands.

grounding: Illustrates a candidate collecting courses, channels and PDFs and feeling busy, but never finishing any, so little is retained.

subtype: Approach: mock tests followed by error analysis [Action]
passage: Every Sunday at 9, Joseph sat at the table on the verandah of his family's house in Thrissur and took a full three-hour mock for the railway recruitment exam. His friend Pranav, preparing for the same exam, came over after lunch to check answers with him. Then came the part Joseph liked most: sorting. Every wrong answer went into one of three columns on a sheet. Concept gap: didn't know it. Silly error: knew it, marked the wrong option. Time: never reached it. This week: concept gaps 6, silly errors 11, time 4. "Eleven silly ones," Pranav said. "That's the biggest." Joseph nodded. "So this week isn't new chapters. It's slowing down. I'll underline the key word in each question and check every calculation once." The next Sunday, silly errors fell to five.

qa.q: How many silly errors were there this week?
qa.a: Silly errors 11.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel about the sorting?
qa.a: Joseph enjoys it, finding it the part he likes most, since it shows exactly where marks are lost.

qa.q: What else could Joseph track over several Sundays?
qa.a: He could chart the three counts week after week, to see which kind of error is shrinking and which needs attention next.

qa.q: How does Pranav help the process?
qa.a: Pranav checks the answers with Joseph and points out the largest column, which helps focus the next week.

grounding: Shows an aspirant taking a full mock every Sunday, sorting wrong answers into concept gaps, silly errors and time problems, and planning around the largest.

subtype: Approach: mock tests followed by error analysis [Action]
passage: In Kaito's small apartment in Osaka, Sunday mornings belonged to the mock exam. Three hours, phone in the other room, kitchen timer on the desk. His friend Jin, preparing for the same national certification exam, did the same across town, and at 2 pm they called each other. First the scores, then the real work. Kaito read out his wrong answers and sorted them aloud: "Question 14, never learned that law: concept gap. Question 22, misread 'not': careless. Questions 58 to 60, ran out of time." This week the tally was concept gaps 9, careless 4, time 7. "Concepts are biggest," Jin said. "So next week, two new chapters and fewer practice sets?" Kaito wrote the plan on the whiteboard: labour law and contracts, three days each. He also set a rule for the time problem: move on after ninety seconds.

qa.q: What time did Kaito and Jin call each other?
qa.a: At 2 pm.

qa.q: How does Kaito seem to feel about sorting mistakes aloud?
qa.a: Kaito seems calm and focused, treating wrong answers as useful information rather than something to feel bad about.

qa.q: What else could Kaito do about the time problems?
qa.a: Kaito could practise short timed sections midweek, so pacing improves alongside the new chapters.

qa.q: How does Jin's weekly call help Kaito?
qa.a: Jin gives a regular partner to review with and helps name the biggest category, making the next week's plan clearer.

grounding: Illustrates an aspirant taking a weekly mock, sorting errors into concept, careless and time categories, and planning the next week around the largest.

subtype: Approach: comparing with toppers' routines [Pitfall]
passage: Amandeep, you asked why I disappeared for two weeks in March. I'll tell you straight. I'm Sahil. I watched a video where last year's topper described his day: up at 4, eighteen hours of study, no phone, no friends. I thought, if he did it, I have to. So I copied it exactly. Day one felt heroic. By day four I was dozing at my desk at 2 pm and reading the same line five times. By day ten I couldn't get out of bed at all, and I felt like the biggest failure alive. Then my mother said something that stuck: "That boy lived next door to his coaching centre and had no job. You tutor children every evening." She was right. His routine wasn't built for my life or my energy. Now I study eight honest hours around my tutoring, and I actually remember things.

qa.q: What time did the topper wake up?
qa.a: Up at 4.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel by day ten?
qa.a: Sahil was exhausted and felt like a complete failure, unable even to get out of bed.

qa.q: What else could Sahil take from toppers without copying them?
qa.a: Sahil could borrow one useful habit, like regular revision, and fit it into a routine that suits Sahil's energy and tutoring work.

qa.q: How does Sahil's mother see the copied routine?
qa.a: Sahil's mother sees that the topper's life was very different, and gently points out it never fit Sahil's situation.

grounding: Shows a candidate copying a topper's eighteen-hour routine, burning out in ten days and feeling a failure, though the routine never matched their life or energy.

subtype: Approach: comparing with toppers' routines [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Abhinav, and I share a room with Jomon, so I saw it start and stop. Jomon had read an interview with the state topper, who said she studied eighteen hours a day. The next morning Jomon's alarm rang at 3:30. He printed the topper's timetable and pasted it above his bed. For about a week he looked unstoppable: books at 4, lunch at the desk, lights off at 11:30. By the eighth day he was falling asleep over his notes by mid-morning and snapping at me for making tea too loudly. On the tenth day he didn't get up at all. He lay there under the timetable and said, "I'm just not made for this." I don't know everything he was feeling. But the topper lived at home with her parents cooking for her; Jomon cooks for both of us and works weekends at a café.

How was Jomon feeling on the tenth day?
qa.a: Jomon felt defeated and hopeless, saying he was just not made for this.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see the topper's routine compared with Jomon's life?
qa.a: Abhinav notices the topper had meals cooked at home while Jomon cooks and works weekends, so the routine never matched Jomon's life.

grounding: Illustrates a candidate copying a topper's eighteen-hour routine, burning out within ten days and feeling a failure, when the routine never fit his life.

subtype: Approach: emotion-aware planning for slumps [Revision]
passage:
Sunday night
Looked at my mock scores for the last two months side by side. There's a pattern and I hate it: every time I've had a week of 2 am nights, the next Sunday's accuracy drops. 71%, 72%, then 64% after the late week. 70%, then 61% after the other late week.
Urmila said it last month and I didn't listen: "You're studying tired, not studying more."
So, new rules from tomorrow:
Lights off at 11. Fixed. Even if a chapter is half done.
A 20-minute walk to the park and back at 6 pm, no phone.
Friday evening off. Completely. A film with Urmila, or sleep.
Two Sundays later, adding this:
The first week felt like wasting time. The second week's mock: 74%. My best yet. I'm annoyed that Urmila was right, and relieved.
Ayesha

qa.q: What time are lights off under the new rules?
qa.a: Lights off at 11.

qa.q: How does Ayesha feel about the 74% result?
qa.a: Ayesha feels relieved and a little annoyed that Urmila was right about studying tired.

qa.q: What else could Ayesha watch for in the coming weeks?
qa.a: Ayesha could keep noting sleep and scores side by side, so any new dip is spotted early.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Ayesha's change?
qa.a: Urmila, whose warning was ignored at first, would likely be glad to see it heeded and to share Friday evenings.

grounding: Shows an aspirant noticing that scores dip after sleepless weeks, adding fixed sleep, an evening walk and a free evening, and seeing accuracy improve.

subtype: Approach: a study partner as accountability [Action]
passage: Hemant and Mahima met in the district library's study hall, two aspirants for the state public service exam who sat at the same long table every day. In week two, Mahima suggested a deal. Every morning at 7, each would message the other three targets for the day. Every night at 10, each would reply with what got done: done, not done, or half. No lecturing, no parents involved, just the two of them. Hemant's first morning message read: "Modern history ch 4 and 5. 40 quant questions. One essay outline." At 10 pm: "Done, done, not done. Outline tomorrow." Some nights he'd rather not send the message, but knowing Mahima would notice a missing one kept him honest. After a month, the librarian noticed they were the last two to leave every evening. Neither had skipped a day.

qa.q: What time do they send morning targets?
qa.a: Every morning at 7.

qa.q: Why does Hemant still send the night message on hard days?
qa.a: Hemant would sometimes rather skip it, but feels accountable, knowing Mahima would notice a missing message.

qa.q: What else could make the partnership stronger?
qa.a: They could add a short Sunday check on the week's targets, to adjust plans together rather than just ticking days.

qa.q: How might Mahima experience the deal?
qa.a: Mahima gets the same steady nudge, with support that feels friendly rather than like pressure from home.

grounding: Shows two aspirants messaging each other their day's targets each morning and results each night, which makes skipping harder without parental pressure.

subtype: Approach: a study partner as accountability [Action]
passage:
Subject: accountability partners? (no pressure, just a message)
Hi Dolma,
We met at the mock test centre last Sunday, the one with the broken fan. You said you keep skipping days, and honestly, so do I. I have an idea.
Every morning by 8, we each send the other one message: today's targets, three at most. Every night by 10, we send what got done. That's it. No advice unless asked, no judging, and we don't involve our families. My parents already ask enough!
I think it works because someone simply knows. When nobody knows I've skipped, skipping is easy. If you're waiting for my message, it's harder.
If we both miss twice in a week, we meet for tea and fix the plan, not blame each other.
Want to try it for two weeks, starting Monday?
Uma

qa.q: Where did Uma and Dolma meet?
qa.a: At the mock test centre, the one with the broken fan.

qa.q: Why does Uma think the idea will work?
qa.a: Uma admits skipping days too and hopes that having Dolma expect a message will make skipping harder.

qa.q: What else could they agree before starting?
qa.a: They could agree what counts as a fair target, so neither sets impossible lists and feels bad every night.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel receiving the email?
qa.a: Dolma, who also keeps skipping days, may feel relieved to find someone in the same spot offering support without pressure.

grounding: Illustrates an aspirant proposing a study partner who exchanges daily targets each morning and results each night, keeping families out of it.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for a poor attempt [Thinking]
passage: Three weeks before the engineering services exam, Irfan's grandfather fell ill, and Irfan spent most days at the hospital in Aligarh instead of at his desk. One evening on the hospital bench, he let the question in: what if the exam goes badly? Instead of pushing it away, he opened a note on his phone. "If it goes wrong: 1. The state engineering exam in August, mostly the same syllabus. 2. The postgraduate entrance in February. 3. Apply to the two firms that came to campus; they hire through the year." His friend Lakshmi, preparing for the same exam, called that night. "You sound calmer," she said. "I made a Plan B, C and D," he told her. "It's strange. Knowing one bad day isn't the end makes me less scared of the day." He revised for an hour on the bench before visiting hours ended.

qa.q: When is the state engineering exam?
qa.a: In August.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after making the backup list?
qa.a: Irfan felt calmer and less scared, knowing one bad day wouldn't be the end.

qa.q: What else could Irfan do with the backup plan?
qa.a: Irfan could note the dates and forms for each route, so switching quickly is easy if needed.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi notice the change?
qa.a: Lakshmi hears it in his voice on the call and says he sounds calmer.

grounding: Shows a candidate quietly working out backup routes, such as a second exam, a postgraduate entrance or a job, so one bad day is not the end.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for a poor attempt [Thinking]
passage: On the local train home to Borivali, Nilesh did something he had avoided for months. He opened a blank page in his notebook and wrote at the top: "If prelims doesn't happen this year." His heart thumped just writing it. Then he made himself continue. Option one: the state civil services exam in October, with a lot of overlap. Option two: the MA entrance in spring, since he liked political science anyway. Option three: a job at the policy research firm where his friend Hansa worked, which had asked for his resume twice. By Dadar the page was full. He noticed his shoulders had come down. The prelims was still the plan. But it was no longer the only door, and somehow that made studying for it feel lighter. That night, when Hansa texted "how's prep?", he replied, "Good. I have exits now."

qa.q: What did Nilesh write at the top of the page?
qa.a: If prelims doesn't happen this year.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel while writing the heading?
qa.a: Nilesh felt anxious, his heart thumping just writing it.

qa.q: What else could Nilesh do to keep the backups ready?
qa.a: Nilesh could note the deadlines for each option and send the resume to Hansa's firm, so the options stay real.

qa.q: How might Hansa see Nilesh's reply?
qa.a: Hansa may be pleased and relieved to hear him sound settled, and glad the firm is one of his exits.

grounding: Illustrates a candidate writing down backup routes such as another exam, a postgraduate entrance or a job, so one poor attempt would not end everything.

subtype: Approach: adaptive replanning after a plateau [Revision]
passage: Last year my mock scores sat at 118 out of 200 for five straight weeks. I'm Nikita. I kept doing what I'd always done: a new chapter every two days, a mock every Sunday. Nothing moved. My friend Afreen said, "Maybe adding more isn't the answer." It annoyed me, because she was right. So I stopped. No new topics for two weeks. I went through my last six mocks and listed every chapter where I'd lost marks more than twice: ratios, seating puzzles, reading comprehension. Two weeks of only those. Then I took my test sheets to Mr. Khanna at the institute and asked him to watch how I attempted a paper. He noticed straight away that I did the hardest section first and panicked. "Start with English," he said. My next mock: 131. Looking back, the plateau wasn't telling me to work harder. It was telling me to work differently.

qa.q: What was Nikita's score for five weeks?
qa.a: 118 out of 200.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about Afreen's suggestion?
qa.a: Nikita felt annoyed at first, precisely because Afreen was right.

qa.q: What else could Nikita do if scores stall again?
qa.a: Nikita could repeat the same check: pause new topics, list repeatedly weak chapters, and ask a teacher to watch a timed attempt.

qa.q: How did Mr. Khanna help?
qa.a: Mr. Khanna watched Nikita attempt a paper and spotted the panic from starting with the hardest section, giving a simple change.

grounding: Shows an aspirant whose mock scores stall stopping new topics, spending two weeks on weak chapters, and asking a teacher to review test strategy.

subtype: Approach: adaptive replanning after a plateau [Revision]
passage:
Coaching faculty note, Karthik (weekend batch), 14 October.
Karthik's mock scores have stayed between 142 and 146 out of 250 for four weeks, while he kept starting new units. Today he came to me with his friend Suraj and six marked test papers. He had already done something sensible on his own: he stopped adding topics last Monday and listed the chapters where he loses marks again and again. Geometry, data sufficiency and para-jumbles.
He asked me to look at his test strategy. I watched him attempt a sectional test. He spends too long proving each geometry answer instead of eliminating options, and leaves para-jumbles to the last five minutes.
We agreed: two weeks of only those three chapters, plus a rule to move on after ninety seconds. I'll review his next two mocks with him personally.
Update, 28 October: 158.
